passages.t: Love in everyday life: strangers, prisoners, marriage, money
passages.happening:
“Continue in brotherly love. Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some people have entertained angels without knowing it. Remember those in prison as if you were bound with them, and those who are mistreated as if you were suffering with them” (verses 1-3).

“Marriage should be honored by all and the marriage bed kept undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers” (verse 4).

“Keep your lives free from the love of money and be content with what you have, for God has said: ‘Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.’ So we say with confidence: ‘The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?’” (verses 5-6).
passages.hearers:
After the great vision of Mount Zion, the letter comes down into ordinary life: the kitchen, the prison, the bedroom and the purse.

‘Brotherly love’ is love for fellow believers, the family of faith. ‘Hospitality to strangers’ is, in Greek, ‘love of strangers’. Inns in the Roman world had a bad name, and travelling believers depended on Christian homes. Opening your door was costly and sometimes risky.

Prisoners in the Roman world often depended on friends and family for food and care. Visiting them could make others suspect you. The readers had done it before (10:34). ‘As if you were bound with them’ asks them to feel a prisoner's chains as their own.

Marriage is to be honoured ‘by all’, not only by married people. ‘The marriage bed kept undefiled’ means faithfulness: sex belongs within marriage, and adultery breaks a covenant.

Then money. The love of money is the opposite of contentment. And the reason to be content is not that we have enough things, but that we have God: ‘Never will I leave you.’
passages.ot:
‘Entertained angels without knowing it’ recalls Abraham, who ran to welcome three strangers at his tent and found that he was receiving the LORD and his messengers: “And Abraham looked up and saw three men standing nearby. When he saw them, he ran from the entrance of his tent to meet them” (Genesis 18:2). Lot also welcomed two visitors who were angels (Genesis 19).

The promise in verse 5 was spoken to Joshua: “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Joshua 1:5), and Moses said it to all Israel: “He will never leave you nor forsake you” (Deuteronomy 31:6). Hebrews gives it to every believer.

Verse 6 quotes a psalm: “The LORD is on my side; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?” (Psalm 118:6).

And Proverbs prays for contentment: “Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the bread that is my portion” (Proverbs 30:8).
passages.hard:
Verse 4 says God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers. What does it ask of us, and what does it not ask?

It asks every believer to honour marriage: to keep faith with a husband or wife, and not to treat another person's marriage lightly. It says that God takes broken promises and sexual wrong seriously. And the whole letter has shown that God's mercy in Christ reaches people who have failed and turn to him.

It does not ask anyone to stay in danger. Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

And verse 5 is not a promise that God will make anyone rich, nor a rebuke of people who are poor. It is a call to be free from the love of money, whatever we have. If you are in money trouble now, look for a trusted adviser where you live; these notes are not financial advice.
passages.asks: Love takes shape in ordinary places. Ask who the strangers are that you could welcome. Ask who is in prison or being mistreated, and how you could stand with them. Ask how you honour marriage, your own or others'. And ask whether money has a hold on you, and what it would mean to be content because God will never leave you.

passages.t: Remember your leaders; Jesus is the same
passages.happening:
“Remember your leaders who spoke the word of God to you. Consider the outcome of their way of life and imitate their faith” (verse 7).

“Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (verse 8).

“Do not be carried away by all kinds of strange teachings, for it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace and not by foods of no value to those devoted to them” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
‘Remember your leaders’ seems to mean leaders from the past, those who first brought the readers the gospel, perhaps now dead. ‘Consider the outcome of their way of life’: look at how their lives ended, faithful to the last, and copy their faith. Not every detail of their lives, but their trust in God.

Then a sentence that stands like a pillar in the middle of the chapter: ‘Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.’ Leaders come and go. Jesus does not. The one who saved them yesterday is the same one who holds them today and will hold them forever.

‘Strange teachings’ about ‘foods’ are not explained. They may have been about Jewish food laws, about eating meals from sacrifices, or about some other food rules. The writer does not attack the readers' heritage. His point is that the heart is made strong by God's grace, not by what a person eats or does not eat.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament honours faithful leaders and asks the people to remember them. Moses told Israel, “Remember the days of old” (Deuteronomy 32:7), and the psalms recall leaders who walked with God.

‘The same yesterday and today and forever’ echoes what the psalms say of God himself: “But You remain the same, and Your years will never end” (Psalm 102:27), words Hebrews applied to the Son in its first chapter (1:12).

Israel's food laws were God's gift to set Israel apart (Leviticus 11). The writer does not mock them. He says the heart is strengthened by grace.
passages.hard:
‘Imitate their faith.’ What if a leader I admired failed badly, or harmed people?

This verse asks believers to look at the ‘outcome’ of a leader's life and copy their faith. It does not ask anyone to copy everything a leader did, or to defend a leader who did wrong. Some leaders who once seemed faithful have fallen, and some have done great harm. When that happens, the harm must be named and the people hurt must be cared for and protected. A leader's gifts never excuse a leader's sins.

And verse 8 gives the deeper answer. Leaders fail; ‘Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.’ Faith does not finally rest on any human leader, however good. It rests on him.

If you have been harmed by a controlling leader or church, what was done was wrong, and it was not your fault. You are free to step away and to tell someone you trust. If you were abused in other ways, or a crime was done, it should be reported to the authorities. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Jesus Christ is the same. Ask whose faith you have learned from, and whether you have thanked God for them. Ask where your faith has leaned too heavily on a human leader. And ask what it means for you today that Jesus is the same as he was yesterday, and will be the same tomorrow.

passages.t: Outside the camp, with sacrifices of praise
passages.happening:
“We have an altar from which those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat” (verse 10).

“Although the high priest brings the blood of animals into the Holy Place as a sacrifice for sin, the bodies are burned outside the camp. And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood” (verses 11-12).

“Therefore let us go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore. For here we do not have a permanent city, but we are looking for the city that is to come” (verses 13-14).

“Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name. And do not neglect to do good and to share with others, for with such sacrifices God is pleased” (verses 15-16).
passages.hearers:
The writer uses the Day of Atonement one last time. On that day the blood of the sin offerings was carried into the Most Holy Place, but the bodies of the animals were not eaten. They were taken ‘outside the camp’ and burned. Places outside the camp were where the unclean and the condemned were sent.

Jesus was crucified outside the walls of Jerusalem, in the place of shame. He was treated as one who did not belong. The writer says: go out to him there. Share his disgrace. The readers were being pushed to the edges of their society for following Jesus. The writer says that is where Jesus is.

‘We have an altar’ most likely means the cross, the place of Christ's sacrifice. Some readers also think of the Lord's Supper. ‘Those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat’ is hard. The writer has just said that the sin offering of the Day of Atonement was not eaten at all. His point seems to be that Christ's sacrifice is of that kind: it is received by faith, not by eating sacrificial meals. Readers differ on the details, and the writer does not explain further.

Then two new kinds of sacrifice. Animals are no longer needed. Believers offer ‘a sacrifice of praise’, words that confess Jesus, and the sacrifice of doing good and sharing with others.
passages.ot:
The rule about the sin offering is in Leviticus 16: the bull and the goat, “whose blood was brought into the Most Holy Place to make atonement, must be taken outside the camp; and their hides, flesh, and dung must be burned up” (Leviticus 16:27). And in Leviticus 6: “But no sin offering may be eaten if its blood has been brought into the Tent of Meeting to make atonement in the Holy Place; it must be burned” (Leviticus 6:30).

Outside the camp was also a place of meeting with God. Exodus remembers a time when Moses “used to take the tent and pitch it at a distance outside the camp”, and “anyone inquiring of the LORD would go to the Tent of Meeting outside the camp” (Exodus 33:7).

The sacrifice of praise and the ‘fruit of lips’ come from Israel's own Scriptures: “Sacrifice a thank offering to God” (Psalm 50:14), and the prophet Hosea's call to say to the LORD, “Take away all our iniquity and receive us graciously, that we may present the fruit of our lips” (Hosea 14:2).
passages.hard:
‘Let us go to Him outside the camp.’ Does this mean leaving Judaism behind with contempt, or that Jewish people have no place with God?

No. ‘The camp’ here is a picture drawn from the Day of Atonement. It names the place of safety, honour and belonging, and the call is to leave the safety of social respect to stand with Jesus where he was rejected. Some readers think the writer was urging Jewish believers not to retreat into the safety of the synagogue to avoid suffering. Others read ‘the camp’ more widely, as any place of safety and status a believer might cling to instead of Christ. Either way, the call is to bear disgrace with Jesus, not to heap disgrace on anyone else.

‘Those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat’ is about the kind of sacrifice Christ's is, not a verdict on a people. The writer has just said that even Israel's priests did not eat the Day of Atonement offering.

For centuries some Christians used this letter, with other parts of the New Testament, to teach contempt for Jews and Judaism. That reading is false. This site rejects it. The note on Acts 2:22-28 sets out why. And notice who is called to go outside the camp: ‘let us go’. The writer includes himself.
passages.asks: Jesus suffered outside the gate. Ask where you are clinging to respectability instead of standing with Jesus. Ask whose disgrace you might share for his sake, people pushed to the edges as he was. And ask what sacrifices of praise and of sharing you could offer this week.

passages.t: Leaders who watch over souls; pray for us
passages.happening:
“Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they watch over your souls as those who must give an account. To this end, allow them to lead with joy and not with grief, for that would be of no advantage to you” (verse 17).

“Pray for us; we are convinced that we have a clear conscience and desire to live honorably in every way. And I especially urge you to pray that I may be restored to you soon” (verses 18-19).
passages.hearers:
Verse 7 spoke of leaders in the past. Verse 17 speaks of leaders now.

‘They watch over your souls’ is a picture of a shepherd who stays awake to guard the flock at night. ‘As those who must give an account’: these leaders are not answerable to no one. They answer to God for how they care for his people.

‘Allow them to lead with joy and not with grief’ asks the church to make its leaders' work a joy and not a burden.

Then the writer asks them to pray for him. He does not stand above them. He needs their prayers. He says his conscience is clear and he wants to live honourably. Something is keeping him away from them, and he asks them to pray that he may come back soon.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament holds shepherds of God's people to account. Ezekiel spoke against leaders who used the flock for themselves: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves! Should not the shepherds feed their flock?” (Ezekiel 34:2). And God promised a true shepherd: “I will appoint over them one shepherd, My servant David, and he will feed them” (Ezekiel 34:23).

Behind every human shepherd stands the LORD: “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” (Psalm 23:1).
passages.hard:
‘Obey your leaders and submit to them.’ Does this mean believers must do whatever a pastor or elder says?

No. This verse has been used to demand unquestioning obedience, to treat every question as rebellion, and to tell people harmed by a leader to stay quiet and submit. That is a misuse.

Read it in its place. It asks believers to trust and work with their leaders because those leaders ‘watch over your souls’ and ‘must give an account’ to God. It assumes leaders like those of verse 7, who spoke God's word and whose faith was worth copying. And it stands under ‘that great Shepherd of the sheep’ (verse 20), to whom every leader answers. It describes the willing trust of a sheep toward a true shepherd, not blind obedience. The New Testament tells leaders not to be “lording it over those entrusted to you” (1 Peter 5:3), and when human commands and God's conflict, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). Churches arrange leadership differently, with bishops, elders or the whole congregation deciding, but across traditions this verse has been read as a call to trust, not to silence. Submission does not mean silence. It is right to ask questions and to expect leaders to welcome being held to account.

And nothing in this passage shields a leader who does harm. Christians agree that leaders are servants accountable to Christ and to his word, and that no authority may be used to cover abuse. If a leader uses his place to control, exploit or harm, these verses do not protect him. Anyone harmed by a church leader is free to speak to another trusted leader, a counselor, or, where a crime is involved, the authorities. Abuse and other crimes are reported to the police and the proper authorities. A church meeting is never a substitute for that. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Good leaders watch over souls and answer to God. Ask how you can make the work of faithful leaders a joy and not a burden. Ask whether you pray for them, as this writer asked. And if you lead others in any way, ask whether you lead as one who must give an account.

passages.happening:
“Now may the God of peace, who through the blood of the eternal covenant brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great Shepherd of the sheep, equip you with every good thing to do His will. And may He accomplish in us what is pleasing in His sight through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen” (verses 20-21).

“I urge you, brothers, to bear with my word of exhortation, for I have only written to you briefly” (verse 22).

“Be aware that our brother Timothy has been released. If he arrives soon, I will come with him to see you. Greet all your leaders and all the saints. Those from Italy send you greetings. Grace be with all of you” (verses 23-25).
passages.hearers:
The letter ends with a blessing, one of the richest in the New Testament. It gathers up the whole message. God is ‘the God of peace’. He ‘brought back from the dead’ our Lord Jesus; here the letter speaks plainly of his rising. Jesus is ‘that great Shepherd of the sheep’, the shepherd over every human shepherd of verse 17. ‘The eternal covenant’ is the new covenant of chapters 8 to 10, sealed with his blood. And the prayer is that God will ‘equip you’ to do his will, and do in us what pleases him. The work is God's from beginning to end.

‘My word of exhortation’ is the writer's own name for his letter. The same phrase is used in Acts 13:15 for a sermon in a synagogue. ‘I have only written to you briefly’ may make modern readers smile, but the letter takes less than an hour to read aloud, and the writer clearly had much more to say.

Timothy, Paul's friend, ‘has been released’, probably from prison, though no other record of this survives. ‘Those from Italy send you greetings’ may mean people in Italy, or people from Italy living elsewhere and greeting friends at home. The letter does not say where it was written from or to.

And the last word is grace.
passages.ot:
‘Brought back from the dead ... that great Shepherd of the sheep’ echoes Isaiah's memory of the exodus: “Where is He who brought them through the sea with the shepherds of His flock?” (Isaiah 63:11). The God who brought Israel up out of the sea brought Jesus up from the dead.

‘The blood of the eternal covenant’ recalls the promise in Zechariah: “As for you, because of the blood of My covenant, I will release your prisoners from the waterless pit” (Zechariah 9:11).

And ‘the God of peace’ is the God of shalom, whom Israel's priests asked to give his people peace in the great blessing: “may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace” (Numbers 6:26).
passages.asks: The last words are a blessing and grace. Ask what it means that the God who raised Jesus will ‘equip you with every good thing to do His will’. Ask what this letter has urged on you, and whether you have borne with it. And receive its last word for yourself: ‘Grace be with all of you.’
